articles.title: Serbia's veteran ruler concedes defeat to student-led movement in snap election
articles.summary: Vucic is a relentless campaigner (SASA DJORDJEVIC) The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Sunday, rose from the wreckage of strongman Slobodan Milosevic's cabinet to the centre of power using his brand of populist nationalism. For supporters, the 56-year-old represented stability, development and patriotism in a country scarred by the bloody wars of the 1990s and ensuing international isolation. But opponents saw him as an increasingly authoritarian figure, twisting between the Kremlin and Brussels and leading a government accused of endemic corruption. Vucic conceded his party had lost after voters cast ballots in record numbers in Sunday's vote, defeated by a new political force that emerged from a years-long protest movement. "Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections," Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. - Political turnaround - Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998. After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party. He was then a vocal supporter of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both later sentenced to life for genocide and other crimes committed during the Bosnian war. But Vucic underwent a dramatic rebrand in 2008, co-founding the conservative, pro-European Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics since. He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017. Even after polishing his image, Vucic has been reluctant to distance himself from nationalist leanings and far-right associates. He has stopped short of condemning Serbs convicted of atrocities during the 1990s conflicts and looked the other way as pro-government media and political allies openly praised war criminals. Despite trying to deny state involvement in a large funeral gathering for Mladic in the Serbian capital last month, several of his ministers attended, drawing sharp criticism from Brussels. - 'Land of cranes' - A relentless campaigner, he maintained a near-constant presence on pro-government television channels, embracing locals in tiny rural villages and chastising critics during lengthy news conferences. He has cultivated the image of a tireless leader criss-crossing Serbia, attracting investment and creating jobs. At the same time, he has juggled the competing interests of European Union aspirations and Serbia's close ties to Russia. Supporters praised him as a brave defender of Serbian sovereignty, spending billions of euros on defence -- as he warned of foreign influence and pressure from NATO-member neighbours. He often cited Serbia's infrastructure and improved living standards as proof of his success, once pledging to make the country a "land of cranes". From the gleaming waterfront district to the numerous projects unfolding in preparation for Expo 2027, his party's slogan "United Serbia" is plastered on billboards across the capital. - Rail station tragedy - But when a concrete canopy collapsed at a newly renovated train station in 2024 killing 16 people, the accusations of corruption which had dogged many of his signature projects caused an outpouring of anger. Student-led demonstrations calling for transparent investigations drew hundreds of thousands to the streets in the largest protests since the Milosevic era. As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back. Students manning university blockades were labelled tools of foreign powers. In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene", thus meeting a key student demand. "All of this will end on October 25," Vucic said, referring to the protests, at a major pre-election rally in Novi Sad, the city where the canopy had collapsed. oz/al/yad/jj This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/aleksandar-vucic-serbias-veteran-ruler-212043564.html

articles.title: LIV Golf faces a make-or-break deadline — and only 4 players have signed on
articles.summary: Dustin Johnson and other players are considering whether to continue with LIV Golf. ASSOCIATED PRESS One way or another, LIV Golf is in its final days as originally created. The tour began life as a PGA Tour breakaway funded by Saudi Arabia's virtually limitless Public Investment Fund, but now is working to both line up financing and hold onto players in preparation for what league officials have termed "LIV 2.0." With a self-imposed go/no-go deadline nearing, several recent developments have complicated plans for a new version of the league. For players, LIV's chief drawing card was the paychecks with astounding numbers of zeroes. Stars, former stars and non-stars alike all cashed in during LIV's run, earning many millions more than they would have been able to on the PGA Tour or the Europe-based DP World Tour. But when Saudi Arabia cut off funding for LIV in April, the pipeline for those paychecks dried up, and now player after player has decided to take their chances elsewhere. The most notable defection came several weeks ago, when Jon Rahm decided he'd had enough of LIV. Rahm's jump to LIV in late 2023 was a seismic moment in golf history, a declaration that the league was capable of enticing even one of the world's best players. But after three years of absolute domination on LIV and underperformance in majors, Rahm opted to walk away from millions — perhaps even tens of millions — owed to him under his initial contract. Rahm's future plans aren't yet known, but the fact that he was willing to forgo the remainder of his contract is a stark statement on his belief in LIV 2.0. Several other notable players have followed Rahm out the door. In recent days, Ian Poulter announced he would be ending his LIV tenure, expressing gratitude on X for the opportunity: Life update…✍🏼 pic.twitter.com/kdSQIOmxZ0 — Ian Poulter (@IanJamesPoulter) October 23, 2026 Rahm's Legion XIII teammate Tyrrell Hatton also announced he wouldn't be playing in LIV 2.0. Like Rahm, his next event will be the DP World Tour's Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship in early November. Major winners Sergio Garcia and Louis Oosthuizen, among many others, have declared that they intend to pursue other opportunities outside LIV Golf. The defection of so many notable players — in name if not necessarily in current skill — makes the challenge of bringing LIV Golf 2.0 to light that much more difficult. Professional golf on an international scale is a star-driven system, and having notable names in the field is the fastest way to draw attention to an event. Accordingly, LIV's new investor, BC Partners Credit, had set a deadline of Sunday, Oct. 25, for players to commit to the league, though BC has the ability to move that deadline. LIV's own attorneys have suggested in recent bankruptcy hearings that the league would make a decision on its future existence by the end of this month. Several players aren't simply walking away from LIV, however; they're seeking what they claim they're still owed. On Sunday, The Athletic r eported that more than 10 players , led by Masters champions Dustin Johnson and Bubba Watson, are seeking more favorable severance deals from the Public Investment Fund. The unpaid terms of their contracts reportedly total more than $100 million. Johnson's attorney David Cornwell suggested that the players are reluctant to sign on with LIV 2.0 until the remaining obligations of LIV 1.0 reach a satisfactory conclusion. The Athletic reported that the PIF had offered the players two cents on the dollar for the remainder of those contracts, and Cornwell indicated that the PIF's decision to cut off funding for LIV ought to give other sports entities pause. "The PIF was an honorable business partner until what we regard as its abandonment of LIV golfers," Cornwell told The Athletic. "Professional sports leagues and their player unions in the United States, along with sports organizations worldwide, should take notice: the PIF's treatment of LIV golfers may signal how it will treat professional athletes in other sports. How you do one thing is usually how you do everything." At the same time, court documents indicated that many LIV executives were paid hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars in retention payments and bonuses prior to the league's bankruptcy filing this summer. While retention payments aren't uncommon during bankruptcy proceedings, the fact that LIV was paying significant amounts to executives while vendors went unpaid raised questions and opened up the league to external criticism. LIV and BC Partners have developed a plan that could bring in up to $300 million in financing for LIV 2.0, and players would hold a majority ownership stake in the new entity. However, as of the deadline date of Sunday only four players — Richard Bland, Ben Campbell, Brendan Steele and Cameron Tringale — had formally committed to the next iteration of the league. Bryson DeChambeau, a free agent who has been linked to the LIV restructuring in the last few months, has not formally committed to the next version of the league just yet. articles.title: Cornell fraternity member seeks dismissal from Jane Doe's sexual assault lawsuit
articles.summary: The Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, N.Y. (Heather Ainsworth for NBC News) One of the men sued by a former Cornell University student identified as Jane Doe has asked a judge to dismiss the claims against him, arguing that her allegations do not support her broader accusations of rape and sexual assault. Diego Sarabia filed the motion Friday seeking dismissal of all claims against him in the lawsuit Doe filed Sept. 16 in New York state court. Sarabia, who was a member of the Chi Phi fraternity, was one of seven men originally sued by Doe for allegedly participating in a gang rape at the Chi Phi house from Oct. 19 to 20, 2024. Sarabia denies the allegations against him, according to the filing. His attorneys argue that even if the complaint’s factual allegations are accepted as true for the purposes of the motion, the claims against him were filed too late, are legally insufficient, or both. James C. Knox, an attorney for Sarabia, wrote in the motion that as far as the allegations against his client, “this is essentially a lawsuit about a forced kiss.” Knox argued that the conduct Doe attributed to Sarabia did not qualify for the extended statute of limitations she cited for certain sexual offenses. Doe accused Sarabia of grabbing her face, kissing her and snorting ketamine off her body with other fraternity members during a drug- and alcohol-fueled encounter in what was known as the “alumni room” of the fraternity house. “Throughout a sprawling complaint approaching 600 paragraphs, plaintiff repeatedly, collectively and without differentiation accuses seven student defendants of ‘sexual assault and rape,’” Knox wrote in his filing. “Those legally conclusory statements do not substitute for pleaded facts.” Knox argued that the complaint did not allege that Sarabia “supplied her with drugs or alcohol, participated in any of the alleged sexual encounters described elsewhere in the complaint, or was even present for most of the conduct that forms the basis of plaintiff’s broader allegations.” The attorney said that the assault, battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress claims were barred by a one-year statute of limitations and the allegations against Sarabia did not qualify for extensions cited in the complaint. Doe’s attorney Thomas Giuffra declined to comment on Sunday. Giuffra previously agreed to withdraw claims against the acting president of the fraternity’s chapter at the time. Protesters rally in support of Jane Doe at the Ithaca Commons on Oct. 13. (Anna Moneymaker / Getty) The lawsuit inspired calls for a reckoning at the Ivy League institution, where past and current students and community members have accused the administration of not doing enough to protect women from sexual assault. Cornell’s Board of Trustees hired former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates “to lead a comprehensive independent review of how the University prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus.” Doe’s allegations were investigated by Cornell University Police. An internal civil rights investigation led to the expulsion of two students and disciplinary action against others. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to bring charges in November 2024 based on a six-page statement in which Doe described some of the sexual conduct that night as consensual. Van Houten declined to evaluate other investigative materials that had been gathered by investigators, including other witness statements. Gov. Kathy Hochul called the evaluation inadequate and recently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations. James’ office has started that process. The attorney general is expected to hire outside investigators to assist with the effort. Two of the accused men are seeking to disqualify James from overseeing the investigation based on a comment she made on social media about the case before she was tapped to run the probe. They argued the state’s top law enforcement official had prejudged the case. Both challenges are still pending. James has deflected calls to step down from the case and has said she is “committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/cornell-fraternity-diego-sarabia-jane-doe-rcna605519

articles.title: How the conservative Supreme Court has reshaped this year's midterms
articles.summary: Demonstrators hold signs in support of minority voting rights outside the US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on October 15, 2025. - Celal Gunes/Anadolu/Getty Images Voters will pick the winners of next month’s midterm elections, but it is the conservative Supreme Court that has set the rules. Long before early voting got underway to decide control of Congress, the court exerted an unusually profound impact on the election with a series of decisions that have reshaped redistricting, campaign finance regulations, efforts to identify noncitizen voters and mail voting – frequently in a way that has benefited Republicans. Some of those decisions received little attention, like the court’s ruling this month that cleared the way for political parties – and particularly, Republicans – to pour millions more into television advertising in tight races. Others were more notable, like the 6-3 ruling in April that effectively gutted the Voting Rights Act’s power to protect minority voters , and prompted a new round of redistricting in Republican-led states. Various rulings have exposed tensions among the justices that spilled into public view . “The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should,” Justice Elena Kagan said at an event on Tuesday in a remarkably frank critique of the court’s actions. Not all of the court’s decisions have backed the Republican position. Both conservative and liberal justices have been skeptical of efforts by President Donald Trump and his allies to alter mail ballot systems, for instance. Despite Trump’s evidence-free claims of widespread voter fraud, the court in September notably rejected the president’s push to give the US Postal Service the unprecedented power to withhold potentially millions of mail ballots. In June, a 5-4 majority upheld state laws that permit mail ballots to be received a few days after Election Day. Even as he has fixated on alleged problems with mail voting, Trump himself has frequently cast a ballot by mail . Trump nominated three of the court’s nine justices during his first term. None of the three dissented from the court’s USPS decision. “Justice Kagan is wildly off base, as are claims that the Supreme Court’s recent record in election cases has favored Republicans,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, told CNN. “Her claims that the court has somehow undermined democracy are little more than political spin.” If polls indicating that Democrats are poised for a victory next month are correct, then many of the Supreme Court’s recent election rulings may have only a negligible impact on the bottom line. But those following the long game say the impact of the Supreme Court’s decisions over the past year will be felt far beyond November. “It’s critical to look beyond the partisan implications of the court’s decisions related to voting rights and to focus on how the court has undermined the very foundations of our multi-racial democracy,” said Samuel Spital, associate director-counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “In a series of decisions over the last 13 years … a majority of unelected judges on the Supreme Court have dismantled the heart of the Voting Rights Act and put our multi-racial democracy in serious danger.” What Snead described as “wildly off base,” Spital called “clear eyed.” Kagan’s rare criticism of fellow justices The timing of Kagan’s warning, just two weeks before the November 3 election, was notable. “The people of America look around at this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare,” Kagan said at the Catholic University law event last week. “And they’re right.” Named to the Supreme Court by former President Barack Obama more than 16 years ago, Kagan is often viewed as the member of its three-justice liberal wing who is most receptive to compromise with her conservative colleagues. That often manifests in subtle ways, such as her decision not to join particularly pointed dissents written by the court’s other two liberals. But when it comes to election disputes, Kagan has been unsparing both in her dissents and in public appearances. Earlier this year, it was Kagan who wrote the dissent in the hugely important 6-3 decision gutting the Voting Rights Act , warning that the consequences would be “far-reaching and grave.” Asked last year about her favorite opinion she has authored, Kagan pointed to her dissent in another high-profile redistricting case from seven years ago. US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan delivers opening remarks during a House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on July 14. - Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images Speaking at Princeton University in early 2025 , Kagan used similarly stark terms to describe that case, in which the court’s 5-4 decision took federal courts out of the business of deciding challenges to partisan gerrymanders. In that decision written by Chief Justice John Roberts, the court concluded even extreme line drawing for political advantage is “beyond the reach of the federal courts.” “What the court did in that case, I thought, was just a real mistake,” Kagan told her alma mater last year. “The foundation of our democracy is voting, and if the voting rights aren’t equal then how does a system of democracy work?” Kagan noted then that she had written “a lot of voting rights dissents” and that it is “an area that I really care about.” Mapmaking, noncitizens and money The court’s most significant election decision this year came in April in a case called Louisiana v. Callais . With the conservatives aligned against the liberals, the court held that Louisiana’s decision to draw a second Black and Democratic district into the state’s overwhelmingly Republican delegation amounted to an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. That decision set off a series of subsequent emergency rulings in which the court allowed both Louisiana and Alabama to quickly redraw their maps for this election in a way that targeted Democratic-held seats. Those decisions boosted Trump’s unprecedented mid-decade redistricting drive. When the dust settled, Republicans had gained an advantage in nine seats. When Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, suggested in May that the court was rolling over its “principles” in pursuit of influencing the November election, conservative Justice Samuel Alito called the insinuation “insulting.” “What principle has the court violated?” Alito wrote . “The principle that we should never take any action that might unjustifiably be criticized as partisan?” Not all of the redistricting decisions went Republicans’ way. The court three times rejected an effort by Missouri Republicans to draw a Democratic congressman out of his seat. And back in February, with no noted dissent, the court allowed California to use a Democrat-friendly map for this year’s election. Some of the court’s other election decisions have drawn less fire but will nevertheless have an impact. Over a dissent from the three liberal justices, the court last month allowed the Department of Homeland Security to provide citizenship verification to states based on a database critics say is riddled with errors. Trump has fixated on unfounded claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. The administration’s latest litigation on that front, challenging votes cast by some 20,000 Californians the administration believes could be noncitizens, is potentially on a path to Supreme Court review before the election. And the Supreme Court on Thursday allowed New Hampshire officials to limit when voters may use a student ID to receive a ballot, agreeing that a lower court ruling that blocked enforcement of the policy was too close to Election Day.  A recent CNN poll found that Democrats enjoy a 31-point advantage over Republicans among younger adults. The court last week backed a Republican effort to lower television campaign ad rates for political parties, rejecting an appeals court decision that would have subjected the Federal Communications Commission to faster judicial review of its decision making. In a related decision in June, the court erased limits on how much political parties could coordinate with federal candidates. Together, the decisions likely incentivized a move this week by the Republican National Committee to unload over $50 million to help midterm candidates. Kagan blasted the decision in June, noting in dissent that it overruled a 2001 precedent and predicting it would flood more money into campaigns. “For those who think there is too much of it in this country — for those who would prefer even more money to be pumped even more easily into politics despite the danger of corruption,” she wrote, “this overruling is for you.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/25/politics/supreme-court-midterm-rules

articles.title: A strange twist in Alaska's Senate race has Trump's DOJ fighting to block results
articles.summary: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday defended the Justice Department's newly filed lawsuit to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying election results if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses in November. In an at-times contentious interview with CNN’s “State of the Union,” Blanche pointed out that according to the Constitution, Congress can create laws at any time to regulate elections. But when host Dana Bash asked what crime the administration was arguing was being committed, Blanche replied, “It depends.” “There could be a crime,” said Blanche. “But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard. So an Alaskan intends to vote for one candidate, but is confused because of a second candidate with exactly the same name who has voted Democrat his entire life, who donated money to the other Democrat opponent, is running.” Bash pressed Blanche on how it is illegal for two candidates with the same name to be on a ballot at the same time. "It is an obligation of the states to avoid confusion, among other things, confusion in the minds of voters in the election process,” Blanche replied. “So the question is whether Alaska, by allowing this to happen, is violating the law and the federal law and the constitution by allowing confusion in the ballot." The Alaskan Supreme Court in June ruled that both Sullivans may remain on the ballot as the incumbent faces off in a tight reelection battle with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The four-person Senate ranked-choice ballot for the general election specifies that Dan S. Sullivan is a "Registered Republican" and the "incumbent" — no information is listed after Dan J. Sullivan Jr's name. Regardless, in the suit filed Thursday , DOJ argued that Dan J. Sullivan Jr.’s name on the ballot constitutes a purposeful effort to mislead voters. Still, it’s unclear how much the court can do about the Justice Department’s lawsuit. With ballots secret, it is virtually impossible for the Justice Department to identify specific voters and clarify which Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for. Blanche, though, seemed unconcerned about that hurdle. “There are a number of scenarios where it could be obvious that a voter was confused by the way they wrote down candidates,” said Blanche. Republican groups have worked to differentiate between the two Sullivans . President Donald Trump on Friday said the legal challenge was his idea, though Blanche on Sunday declined to state whether the president had directed him to file the suit. "I will never talk about any communications I have with the president of the United States,” he said. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who is not up for reelection this year, said Friday that the lawsuit is unnecessary. “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski said in a post on X . “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.” Her comments drew the ire of Trump, who on Saturday called Murkowski “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far,” in a post to Truth Social . Trump said that Alaska’s ranked choice voting system is “a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.” “He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election, and Murkowski probably wants that to happen, which is why she is against the DOJ filing a Lawsuit in order to stop this impending crime and tragedy,” Trump added. “I have delivered for Alaska at Historic Levels, nobody has ever seen anything like it, and all I’m asking for is a FAIR AND HONEST SENATORIAL ELECTION! Lisa Murkowski is a DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country. You just don’t get any worse!" Democratic leaders have also widely condemned the lawsuit, arguing the president is attempting to lay the foundation to overturn the midterm election results if their candidates win critical elections — something Bash asked Blanche about on Sunday. “One of the big questions is whether or not the president is laying the groundwork for a scenario where, whether it's Alaska or somewhere else, there is, in your words a couple of days ago, a 'doomsday scenario' and we could be in a situation where President Trump tries to overturn the election and the result of that could be, god forbid, what we saw after January 6th,” Bash said. Blanche quickly fired back: “Oh stop it. You gotta stop it with that. You're not being a real person. You set me up. You're saying, “'Mr. Attorney General, because the president of the United States wants to stop fraud and confusion in Alaska, is he going to do something crazy?' That is not a real question.” Bash replied that she did not think it was an unfair question, but Blanche argued that the premise of the question was untrue. “Instead of focusing on how we can address that and how we can remedy that, you're talking about January 6th,” he said. “That's so embarrassing to this network that that's what you're talking about.” “Oh, come on,” Bash said. "Don't “oh, come on” me,” replied Blanche. “There's literally confusion." It wasn’t the only tense interview Blanche had Sunday. In an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” Blanche accused host Margaret Brennan of lying over the wording of the Justice Department’s lawsuit . “The Alaska Supreme Court did take on this matter,” Brennan began, referring to the court’s June decision. “No, they didn't. That's a state law,” interrupted Blanche. “In this country, the states administer the elections. This is how the state came up with the issue and how to handle any confusion,” Brennan said as the Alaskan ballot was shown on the screen. “You’re not telling the truth,” said Blanche. Brennan asked why identifying Sullivan as the incumbent is insufficient for the administration. “Well, listen, I don't know if it's sufficient,” said Blanche. “But I can tell you this: that the director of the Alaska election system has said that it will likely cause confusion.” Brennan pointed out that the ballots are already circulating, and voting may already be underway, as many vote by mail in Alaska. She then pressed Blanche on Trump claiming responsibility for the lawsuit, to which Blanche reiterated that he will not share his communications with the president. “The president of the United States said this on camera ,” Brennan replied. “He said, "I told them to do it." Did he tell that to you?” “He didn’t say that on camera,” argued Blanche, before adding Trump had been looking at the situation for “months and months and months.” He later added that he had “no idea” who Trump was referring to, and even if he did, he would “most certainly not” talk about it. Brennan then pivoted to read several lines from DOJ’s lawsuit, including that the suit defined voter confusion as Sen. Sullivan not winning the election and that had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast for the incumbent then he would have won. As she spoke, Blanche interrupted again. “That’s not what it says,” he said. “I’m quoting from it,” Brennan replied, holding up a printed version of the suit. “You are telling them not to certify it. What right does the federal government have telling a state not to certify or how to certify?” After a moment of crosstalk, Blanche stated: "If you talk the whole time you're not going to get answers out of me. If you let me answer your question I can address your question." He then said the suit does not call for officials to avoid certifying the election. “All we're doing is trying to put guardrails in place so that if that happens there's a system allowed where the ballots are kept in a way so we can determine whether there was confusion,” he explained. In his interview with CNN, Blanche denied any political motivations were behind the Justice Department’s lawsuit. “It's important the American people understand that we are not — President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape or form,” he said. “What we're trying to do is make it clear that if it is obvious after the election, that confusion led to an improper and illegal result that the Alaskan system should be able to address that.” In an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) argued the administration has no standing to bring the Alaska lawsuit, and he lambasted Blanche for leading a “disgraceful campaign.” “This suit has no chance of succeeding,” said Schiff. “But the fact that Todd Blanche and the Justice Department are willing to go along with it, they're willing to put their name on it, is an indication of how far they will go after this election is over to try to challenge the results.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/25/blanche-alaska-lawsuit-could-be-crime-01134861

articles.title: ICE said a man jumped on the hood of their vehicle. Video — and police — say otherwise.
articles.summary: A Northern California man was responding to a call about ICE activity in his city when surveillance footage showed he was hit by an agent in an SUV on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. - Obtained by CNN When footage of a man being hit by federal immigration officers’ SUV in Northern California became public, the Department of Homeland Security responded by saying the man had jumped on the vehicle’s hood. Local police raised doubts about federal officials’ account as they announced a criminal investigation into Tuesday morning’s incident involving the pedestrian, 37-year-old Antonio Moreida, citing video footage that contradicted DHS’ statement. Footage from a nearby surveillance camera, a bystander’s cellphone recording and Moreida’s GoPro, which had already been made public at the time of the agency’s statement, told a different story of what happened on a residential street in Woodland, an agricultural city just outside of Sacramento. The incident is the latest in which DHS’ account has been contradicted by officials and video evidence amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Police contradict ICE account In a statement Wednesday morning, DHS said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers didn’t hit a pedestrian. “An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement in response to CNN’s request for information. “The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation,” apparently accusing the man of faking his injuries. After the incident on Tuesday, Woodland Police Chief Ryan Kinnan said in a statement he found footage of the incident troubling. Investigators were working to gather evidence and statements and to review available audio and video related to the incident, including video taken from multiple perspectives, police said in a Facebook post . Woodland Police didn’t take part in the ICE operation the agents were involved in that morning, police said. The following day, Woodland Police called DHS’ account “inconsistent.” “Certain claims made in the DHS statement are inconsistent with the video evidence obtained and reviewed by Woodland Police investigators,” Kinnan said in an update Wednesday . The update said investigators had established, based on video evidence, the pedestrian had been hit by the vehicle driven by ICE agents and that he had not jumped onto the vehicle. The local police department is conducting a criminal investigation into the events leading up to the collision and the actions of those involved, Kinnan said Wednesday. By Thursday, in response to follow-up questions about the video footage, federal officials no longer said the person jumped on the hood. “This individual chose to directly impede a law enforcement action and stand in the middle of an active road,” an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to CNN. “Our officers deliberately attempted to avoid making contact with this anti-ice protestor and drive around him, while also braking. We strongly urge individuals to not stand in the middle of active roadways while a law enforcement vehicle is approaching.” What footage shows Footage reviewed by CNN shows Moreida, a Woodland resident, in the middle of the street at around 9:40 a.m. Tuesday. Moreida said he had responded to a call that morning by NorCal Resist, a group which monitors immigration operations, about ICE activity in Woodland, he told CNN on Tuesday, hours after the incident. unknown content item - He said he was trying to record agents’ unmarked vehicles. He had been recording one vehicle, standing on the car’s driver’s side, when it turned left and drove off, which he said pushed him into the middle of the street. Video from Moreida’s GoPro shows him following a black Dodge Durango with tinted windows as it drives down the street. Then, he said he heard a loud engine before seeing the agents’ black Chevy Tahoe drive toward him, which is shown in his GoPro footage, though the video has no audio. unknown content item - Down the street, the bystander’s cellphone video shows the Durango pass the Tahoe, which has tinted windows, on a residential street. In the video’s background, people can be heard blowing whistles, presumably to alert people nearby of ICE’s presence in the neighborhood. The ICE agent driving the Tahoe moves toward Moreida and between the cars with its brake lights on, footage shows. In the bystander’s video, Moreida isn’t yet visible. The SUV’s wheels begin to turn to the left only a few feet from Moreida, a wider angle of surveillance footage from a home shows. unknown content item - “The individual was standing in the street long enough that a reasonable person should be able to see them and recognize that they were there,” said Ryan Schwank , a former ICE attorney and training instructor who reviewed the videos provided by CNN. Schwank also took issue with ICE’s characterization that Moreida was standing in the middle of an active road and impeding law enforcement’s actions. “When we’re looking at Antonio’s actions, he’s not impeding. He’s not standing blocking the vehicle from moving,” he said. “He’s standing and filming, and that’s well within his bounds to do. He’s well within his rights to do what he was doing.” Moreida’s GoPro appears to show when he’s struck by the front-right side of the vehicle before he drops his camera. “Before I knew it, it just drove straight into me,” he said. “I took the hood of the car straight to the chest. It initially took the wind out of me and I couldn’t breathe.” The surveillance footage shows Moreida take a step back when he appears to make contact with the car. He is then seen falling toward the ground, off the front-right side of the car, the footage shows. A bystander's cellphone video shows the moments when an SUV driven by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer hit a man filming federal immigration enforcement operations in Woodland, California, on October 20, 2026. -  NorCal Resist In the bystander’s footage from behind, a screeching noise is heard before the Tahoe jolts forward. The SUV veers left before straightening out, the video shows. The bystander’s angle shows the Tahoe brake lights turn off. Moreida is then visible in the bystander’s video, falling to the ground and rolling, first on his back with his legs swinging above him. He then appears seated upright in the nearby surveillance footage, this time facing the sidewalk. The SUV’s brake lights turn back on briefly before it drives farther down the street, the surveillance footage shows. The driver, an ICE agent, stayed near the scene and called local dispatch, Woodland Police said. The agent cooperated with police during the initial investigation, the local agency said. Moreida said an off-duty EMT provided him aid at the scene before Woodland Police officers arrived. Federal agents didn’t approach him after he was hit by the SUV, he said. Moreida said he was eventually transported to the hospital. He said he had X-rays taken of his swollen knees, where he said he had the most damage. In addition, he said he has bruises and cuts from the road. ICE has reduced the amount of training for officers, including in vehicle operations and how to deal with confrontations, said Schwank, who is now an agency whistleblower after resigning in February . On Saturday, ICE said it is instituting additional training for officers. “ICE training will now be extending to 72 days. The change, effective June 2, 2026, will apply to all new academy classes beginning July 1, 2026. All graduates of the previous academy curriculum will attend follow-on training at the Advanced Field Officer Training Program,” an ICE spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CNN. “As we have said all along, ICE training does not end when recruits graduate from the academy. ICE officers go through a rigorous on-the-job training and mentorship. This additional training is tracked online and monitored closely.” Local officials call for investigations Soon after it became public, local officials expressed dismay over the incident, which occurred in a rural Northern California community that’s about half Latino. More than a fifth of the population is foreign-born, according to US Census estimates . “The lack of truth in the Department of Homeland Security’s statement is evidenced by video taken at the scene,” Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said in a statement issued Wednesday. “All of us can be assured that the Police Department’s investigation into this disturbing incident will continue to be speedy, fair, and impartial.” US Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat whose district includes Woodland, said ICE’s statements about the facts surrounding the incident were disappointing but not surprising. “ICE has a history of trying to hide the facts and mislead the public,” he told CNN. “And this is another example of that happening.” On the day of the operation, Thompson called on Acting ICE Director David Venturella to investigate the collision, including by preserving evidence and cooperating with local authorities. As of Friday, the congressman had yet to receive a response to his letter, his office told CNN. CNN’s Taylor Galgano contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/25/us/woodland-man-struck-by-ice-vehicle

articles.title: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer says America is ready to elect a female president
articles.summary: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back Sunday on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a female president. “Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I’ve heard everyone say, ‘You can’t have this person or that person,’” the governor told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “I would put my money on any Democratic governor in the country against [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio in 2028,” she added, pointing to two Republicans widely expected to run for president in two years. Asked directly whether a woman could be the best choice to beat a potential GOP presidential nominee in 2028, Whitmer simply said, “I do.” In 2025, Obama said in public remarks: “As we saw in this past election, sadly, we ain’t ready. That’s why I’m like, don’t even look at me about running, because you all are lying. You’re not ready for a woman. You are not.” Several women, including Whitmer and former Vice President Kamala Harris, are widely speculated to be potential candidates in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. On Sunday, Whitmer did not deny that she’s exploring a potential run for president in 2028, saying that she’ll decide on her next steps after she departs from her post as governor in January. “When I exit office … I’m going to take a little time off and figure out what I want to do next, so I’ve got nothing new to share with you, unfortunately,” Whitmer told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. Earlier this year, Whitmer denied that she planned to run for president but quickly walked back the comments. “There will be a robust group of people running for president,” she said at the time, adding, “I will not be one of them in 2028, I can tell you that.” Later the same day, the governor said: “I never thought I would run for governor. So I guess I should know better to never say never.” Several other Democratic governors, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, are also widely regarded as potential 2028 presidential candidates. Each has been crisscrossing the country ahead of the midterms campaigning on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidates in competitive races. Whitmer on Sunday highlighted her support for former public health official Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor in Ohio. Earlier this week, Acton’s opponent, GOP businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, released a TV ad featuring Acton’s mother calling her a “liar.” Acton has publicly shared that she’s been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years and has accused her late stepfather of sexually abusing her. Acton and her brother were removed from her mother’s custody in 1978 after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested on a child rape charge. Acton’s mother has not responded to requests for comment. “I’m going to stay focused on getting people like Amy Acton over the finish line. What’s happened to her in Ohio is absolutely abhorrent, and any survivor knows there’s always a backlash. But this is what makes it harder for women to seek help after they’ve been sexually assaulted in this country,” Whitmer said Sunday. “It is unreal what’s going on, and that’s why we’ve got to — we’ve got to win races like this and elect good people who are going to keep the people at the heart of their work, like Dr. Amy Acton.” Ramaswamy’s decision to air the ad has faced widespread bipartisan condemnation , some of it from GOP Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who is locked in a tight re-election race. This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/politics-news/gretchen-whitmer-america-ready-elect-woman-president-acton-rcna605512

articles.title: She blocked his bid to become a federal judge. Now he's running for her Senate seat.
articles.summary: Why are major Democrats and Republicans flocking to Mississippi in recent weeks? In a climate where polls show President Donald Trump's approval ratings cratering, Democrats are unusually optimistic about Scott Colom's chances of flipping the Senate seat held by incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith -- even in deep-red Mississippi. "We got to have a senator that looks out for Mississippi, that puts Mississippi farmers first, Mississippi small businesses first, represent our values by not allowing corruption to ruin our country and actually delivers on the commitments to put America first," Colom told ABC News in an interview earlier this week. Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks during a voting rights town hall at the historic Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. The incumbent's campaign dismisses the Democratic push as the last-ditch effort of a campaign that will fall short. Gov. Wes Moore says key races in South 'in play,' Democrats 'made mistakes' not investing earlier Colom is a district attorney for four counties along the Mississippi-Alabama border and a former nominee to become a U.S. district judge. He would be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. Democrats have argued that Colom's prominent credentials, as well as voter pushback against Republican incumbents and motivation among Democratic-leaning Black voters, could help boost him. Mississippi's population is around 36% Black, according to U.S. Census data . Colom faces an uphill battle, as Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 and voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by around 20 points. ABC News rates the race solid Republican. But he has gotten the attention of national Democrats; major party figures such as former former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock have campaigned with him. Former President Barack Obama also recorded an ad for him released earlier this month. Harris, during a rally with Colom on Thursday, told attendees, "I've been in those rooms where there's no cameras, it's senators talking to each other... When you have a voice like his in that room, just think about the impact that's going to have on the decisions coming out of that room. Think about that. This is no ordinary time, and this is no ordinary man." AP Photo - PHOTO: Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigns for candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi, Oct. 22, 2026. Colom also went viral online last week after a social video he posted showed Hyde-Smith, during a local news interview from February, saying "You have so many proteins to choose from" while discussing how to deal with higher prices on meat and other goods. In the interview, Hyde-Smith also spoke about working on regulations that would help energy production, and tax incentives to help development. But it was the proteins part that Colom's campaign seized on, with a punchy video that featured voters mocking the senator's words, with one saying, "Pick another protein ... I'd rather pick another Senator instead." (The campaign has confirmed to ABC News that the video has been turned into a campaign ad.) Sarah Warnock/AP Photo - PHOTO: Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom listens during a maternal health roundtable at the Capital Club in Jackson, Miss., Aug. 1, 2026. One concrete sign of confidence among Democrats over Colom's chances came on Tuesday, when the Senate Majority PAC, an outside group aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign across broadcast TV and digital for ads for Colom. Asked what signs the group sees in Mississippi that makes it worth investing in, spokesperson Lauren French wrote, "Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent a decade in Washington without passing a single piece of legislation, and Mississippians have noticed." Hyde-Smith has cosponsored legislation that has passed into law but legislation she initially sponsored or reintroduced has not become law, according to congressional records . Asked to respond to Senate Majority PAC, Hyde-Smith's campaign pointed to how bills from lawmakers "are often passed as part of larger legislative packages," and that has been true for some of Hyde-Smith's bills, including the first one she introduced. The campaign also pointed out that she is running for only her second full term. French said Colom is running a "disciplined campaign" with messages resonating with voters. Colom and Hyde-Smith have some history, as she blocked his nomination for federal judge in 2023. She cited his support for transgender rights and having previously been boosted by a George Soros-linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press . He insists his bid for Senate is not motivated by a desire to get back at her. "It has nothing to do with the run for me ... as a Christian, I forgive her. It's about the people in Mississippi," Colom told ABC News. Hyde-Smith dismissed Colom's chances. Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images - PHOTO: Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith arrives in the U.S. Capitol for the first vote of the week, September 22, 2026. "We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith back to the U.S. Senate on November 3rd. This is simply Washington insiders making a last ditch effort to give life to Scott Colom's failing campaign," campaign manager Jake Monssen told ABC News in a statement. Hyde-Smith's supporters may be more motivated after a boost from President Donald Trump, who's set to hold a rally in Mississippi on Monday as part of a swing of campaign rallies mostly in red states. The Republican National Committee announced the rally around a week after Colom's social video went viral, although Trump and the group have not indicated why they are doing the rally there and Trump has expressed confidence in Hyde-Smith. "Cindy Hyde-Smith's very popular ... So if I need to get her over the top, I would go there [to Mississippi]. She's great. Cindy Hyde-Smith is great," Trump told reporters when asked Thursday about the Senate election. Hyde-Smith will be attending the rally, according to her campaign. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/democrats-aim-deep-red-mississippi-senate-seat-scott/story?id=137484924

articles.title: She voted for Trump every time. Then came cancer and the bills.
articles.summary: McALLEN, Texas (AP) — The Ford Expedition rumbled to a stop and Cindy Banda’s bedazzled flip-flops landed on the asphalt of the Houston cancer center’s vast parking lot. She threaded through the rows of cars, a tally of patients who gather here to sit with chemotherapy needles or lie on radiation machines. The elevator dinged open. A year ago in this building, surgeons removed Banda’s right breast, and she still didn't know whether treatment had expunged the cancer from her body. Doctors had told her it would be tough to beat. “I’m more of a positive person myself,” Banda said, now sitting with a white wristband in a dim waiting room. But the bills are harder to dismiss, and the single mother with six children in her care repeated something like a mantra. “Keep the house. Keep the cars. And just keep the kids stable.” That’s true for many Americans, as rising healthcare costs leave more families with a sinking feeling after seeing the bill for surgery or medication. Heading into the Nov. 3 midterm elections, about half of registered voters said healthcare costs are a major problem for them and their families, up from a little more than one-third four years ago, according to a Fox News poll from September. With party control of Congress at stake, registered voters are nearly twice as likely to say they trust Democrats over Republicans to handle healthcare , according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from the same month. Those frustrations, combined with broader concerns over rising prices, have sapped support for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. Banda knows how that feels. She backed Trump in each of his three campaigns, motivated by her opposition to abortion . But when cancer came, the ensuing scramble to make ends meet was painful enough to rearrange her priorities, and she started to think about voting Democratic for the first time. The 46-year-old was ushered into a sterile room for her appointment, her phone lit up with a text. “Please contact TD Auto Finance.” “This one’s $1,300,” she said of the car payment bill. “I have to go back to work.” She had been on sick leave from her job selling internet service for one year, and she needed the income to support her three kids and three more she had taken in after her sister's death. The doctor said her reconstruction surgery could be scheduled early next year. “I was hoping for maybe December,” Banda said, “only because I've met my deductibles.” Come January, she would have to pay down the $7,500 again. Earlier may be possible, the doctor replied, if the skin around her surgical scar loosens. The evening had cooled slightly by the time she walked back through the rows of parked cars, their ebb and flow marking the tide of sickness, survival and death in a small corner of a colossal healthcare industry that saves lives while taking in over $5 trillion every year. Banda paid $8 for parking as she left. Confronting death and debt in America before a midterm election Two weeks later, Banda was back at work, making door-to-door rounds to sell Spectrum's Wi-Fi in McAllen, her city along the U.S.-Mexico border in the Rio Grande Valley. Banda, holding blue flyers, walked along a row of storefronts, some that shuttered since she last was in the area. She hadn't had a sale and commission since October of last year, after the biopsy and diagnosis. The doctor who gave her the news had hugged Banda, and she sobbed even though she never really sobs in front of other people. During chemo, her children took turns buzzing off her wispy hair. When her 9-year-old daughter's hand quivered, a teenage cousin helped guide the clipper over her mother’s scalp. Banda’s first impulse was to maintain normalcy, stability, for the children. But that requires roughly $7,000 a month for utilities, mortgage, car payments and groceries, along with the two water leaks. Then, even with insurance through her job, the surgeries, chemo and radiation added up to over $25,000 that she's been paying off, making Banda one of tens of millions of other people in the United States in medical debt. Banda tries not to dwell on death and debt. “It’ll consume you,” she says. She smothers those thoughts beneath her bubbly demeanor and avoids being alone. But that truce, between her insistence on positivity and the fears that it covers, is brittle. Certain thoughts still arrive uninvited. Banda’s late sister, Melissa, didn’t have life insurance. Banda makes sure it's a payment she never misses. “Sometimes I think, and I shouldn’t think like this, but I’m worth more gone than here,” she said one day. “Obviously, the goal is not that, the goal is to beat it,” she continued, “to keep the house and keep the cars.” So far she has, with the help of others. On top of child support, the father of Banda's 9-year-old often pays $400 a week for a nanny to help with the kids. Banda’s own father sent her $700 before for her recent Houston appointment, one of his many cash infusions. Her high school classmates, who she hadn’t been in close touch with in decades, fundraised by selling grilled chicken, rice and beans from a roadside tent. Two GoFundMe fundraisers raised nearly $30,000 and Banda rented her late sister’s house while putting her own in forbearance. But months of insecurity takes its own, sleepless toll. She needed to sell some internet services to catch up. After sticking the Spectrum Wi-Fi flyers onto empty storefronts, she drove to pick up her kids from school. The following day she had a morning meeting at a barbershop for what would be her first sale back at work. Turning on Trump and voting Democratic for the first time A lifelong Christian, Banda had voted her anti-abortion stance in past elections. When her sister was kidnapped and murdered by her ex-husband in 2020, Banda retreated from religion. The cancer brought her back to church with an apology to God, but it also made her rethink her politics. She voted for Trump in 2016, and his first four years seemed steady, so she voted for him again in 2020. Democratic President Joe Biden's tenure, including the tail end of a global pandemic and rising inflation, felt like bedlam, so she voted for Trump to return to the White House in 2024. But two years later and fighting an expensive disease, she had found no respite from high prices. So when James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminary student running for U.S. Senate as a Democrat, visited one of Banda’s fundraisers — speaking about his diabetes and his work in the Texas Statehouse to lower the price of insulin — it moved her. “Imagine if he can do that for the cancer,” she said. Talarico and his Republican opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, have different approaches to healthcare. Talarico wants all Americans to be able to join Medicare; Paxton proposed a $25,000 tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses. Talarico also supports a law guaranteeing abortion access nationwide, which Banda has voted against for years. But after she slid into debt to stay alive, after her grocery bills mounted and the high school had to comp the kids' soccer gear she couldn't afford, Banda’s anti-abortion concerns have been superseded by costs. “Because it’s what I’m living,” she said. “I'm living it." Banda cast an early ballot for Talarico. “Never voted Democrat before today!!” she wrote in a text with blue heart emoji. Her news will come on Election Day, in a doctor's office Banda had just started a new cancer-targeting medication that cost $16,000 a month, reduced to $500 by insurance. By the afternoon, she was nauseous and fatigued, unable to eat. The malaise would keep her home the next day. She would miss the meeting with the barbershop to close her first deal since getting sick, though she felt confident it was in the bag. But Banda pushed through the discomfort one evening to join her family as they replaced the flowers at her sister's tomb. She drove past the headstones and oak trees in the evening’s slanting light, and the family gathered around Melissa Banda's tomb in an open-air mausoleum. There was no speech. Their eulogy was her father, Fidel Banda, methodically clipping and arranging the flowers for his daughter. Banda walked along the wall of tombs. She will find out on Election Day whether the cancer is in remission or whether it's spread to her organs. “This one’s for me,” she said, pointing to a blank tomb next to her sister's. “Mom!” said her daughter with the huffiness of a 9-year-old. “Why would you say that?” Banda smiled and added, “in a hundred years." This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/she-voted-trump-every-time-123400184.html

法国周末爆发新一轮抗议浪潮，动荡烈火有蔓延欧洲之势，包括反恐部队在内7万安保人员紧急上阵、多城宵禁 。卢浮宫，奥赛博物馆和毕加索博物馆三大热门景点周六闭馆，原定在巴黎举行的巴黎圣日耳曼队与里昂队的足球比赛也被推迟。巴黎市长表示，市政府正为持续数周的长期情况做准备，预计市政厅的损失可能达到数千万欧元。 法国内政部：1314人在新一轮抗议示威中被捕 。内政部公报称，全法有41万人参与周六的新一轮抗议示威活动，其中巴黎地区约11万人；当天全法共有289场抗议示威活动。与此前一周的抗议示威活动相比，本轮抗议示威活动的规模和暴力程度有所减弱。法国工会组织称，约80万人参与了24日的抗议示威活动。 穆迪维持法国信用评级不变，负面展望持续 。穆迪宣布维持法国Aa3评级不变，声明中指出，法国多元化的经济结构与强健的公共机构支撑了现有评级，但同时将展望维持于负面，理由是政治不稳定性将持续制约财政整顿努力。穆迪表示，Aa3评级的维持建立在法国最终通过削减赤字预算方案的基础假设之上，并预计"融资成本与社会紧张态势将在未来数月内有所缓解"。 报道：特朗普政府拟取消部分加拿大商品关税，助力中期选举 。据媒体报道，特朗普政府计划豁免部分加拿大农林产品的50%关税，最早本周五公布。为保持总体关税规模不变，此次减税可能以对其他加拿大商品加征关税的方式加以对冲。此举主要旨在帮助缅因州联邦参议员Susan Collins在中期选举中守住席位，同时可能惠及其他贸易依赖型州的共和党候选人。 美国10月综合PMI初值小幅回落至57.6，企业售价涨幅创四年高位，通胀压力升温 。美国10月综合PMI初值降至57.6，虽较9月回落，但仍处于近五年来高位；服务业PMI降至57.9，制造业PMI升至56.0，创53个月新高。新订单增速创逾四年半新高，就业扩张加快，但企业销售价格涨幅升至2022年8月以来最高，油价、原材料及运输成本上涨加剧通胀压力。 法国PMI全线跌破荣枯线，欧元区10月综合PMI初值降至51.9逊于预期 。受法国财政与政局担忧拖累，其10月综合PMI降至48.4跌入萎缩；德国虽维持扩张但增速放缓，拉低欧元区综合PMI至51.9。法债抛售与高企通胀加剧市场对金融条件收紧的担忧，市场普遍预期欧洲央行或于近期暂停加息。 日本核心CPI年内首破2%，超过80%经济学家预计12月加息 。更受日本央行关注的剔除生鲜食品和能源的深层通胀指标同比上涨2.4%，服务业价格创七个月新高，显示需求驱动型价格压力持续积聚。企业提价潮持续蔓延，10月逾3000种商品涨价。市场预计日本央行12月将再度加息，终端利率或触及2%上方。 韩国股市便宜到全球罕见，成为首个跌破5倍市盈率的万亿美元级市场 。韩国KOSPI指数未来12个月预期市盈率降至仅4.2倍，成为彭博2006年有数据以来首个跌破5倍关口的万亿美元级市场，估值仅略高于正遭MSCI降级风险的雅加达综合指数。AI热潮降温令韩股遭抛售，尽管出口迈向1万亿美元、SK海力士与三星芯片需求旺盛，投资者仍不愿为盈利支付更高价格。 全球投资级企业债利差创一年半新高，AI融资潮冲击信用市场 。美国科技巨头为支撑AI基建大幅举债，叠加油价上涨和法国动荡，推动全球企业债利差急剧走阔。周四全球投资级企业债利差飙升至129个基点，创2025年5月以来最宽水平。分析指出，“如果科技股财报传来好消息，唯一的意涵可能是它们会进一步扩大支出计划。” 美国三大电信股盘前齐跌！SpaceX洽商接入8万基站，剑指全美"第四大运营商" 。SpaceX洽谈接入美国约8万座基站，计划结合卫星网络切入移动通信市场，引发电信股重新定价。AT&T、Verizon和T-Mobile盘前均跌超4%，Crown Castle和American Tower则分别上涨8.6%和6.1%。市场担忧新竞争者冲击传统运营商定价权与利润率，但基站运营商或因新增租赁需求受益。相关合作仍处早期阶段，监管、频谱及商业条款尚存不确定性。 苹果首款折叠屏iPhone Duo出师不利：有人折不到20次就裂屏了 。从中国到美国，再到澳大利亚和加拿大，多个市场都有用户报告类似问题，而且坏的地方几乎都一样：手机中间的折叠区域。 现在苹果需要回答，一部售价2000美元、主打折叠体验的手机，究竟能不能经得起用户每天反复打开和合上？ AI算力远期需求旺盛！亚马逊AWS今明年产能都已被抢空，连2028年的算力都快没了 。亚马逊 CEO Andy Jassy称，AWS的大部分产能已预订至2028年，面对满载的远期订单，其极具弹性的短周期“按需采购”策略成功规避了产能过剩风险。 亚马逊CEO：AI业务年化收入超250亿美元，增速是AWS初期的数百倍，砸2200亿美元仍无法满足需求 。亚马逊CEO Jassy直言，解锁企业级AI大市场必须将推理成本再降十倍，这正是死磕自研芯片的核心逻辑。 高管揭示Meta AI订阅变现新路：Muse免广告但企业服务收费，智能体购物抽成 。Meta AI负责人Alexandr Wang称，Muse对普通用户免费开放，Meta没有投放广告的计划；Meta计划向企业提供付费服务，未披露具体的收费标准和推出时间。他还称，Meta自有的基础设施、安全体系和数据中心使Muse具备对手难以复制的竞争优势。 全网恐慌48小时，拯救互联网的却是一个“无名之辈” 。“有这么一个人，世界上大部分PHP发行版都靠他一个人维护。如果这个人出了什么事，那就完了。所有人都要遭殃。” AI加速“挖漏洞”！网络安全专家警告：未来数月网络安全事件恐频发 。AI正大幅加速软件漏洞发现与攻击工具开发，网络安全防御窗口急剧压缩。本周PHP严重漏洞已导致多个政府网站中断，业内警告，未来数月类似事件可能频繁发生，AI推动今年数字漏洞发现数量同比翻倍。不过，漏洞激增并不必然意味着攻击成功率上升。短期内，企业修复与应急响应压力将加大，长期则可能推动网络安全需求持续扩张。 研报精选 博弈选举，美以伊“下大棋” 。以色列将于10月27日举行议会选举，美国将于11月3日举行中期选举。内塔尼亚胡强硬表态、推动对伊动武，意在争取选举支持；特朗普则顾虑油价上涨冲击共和党选情，对开战释放矛盾信号。伊朗一边加强霍尔木兹海峡管控、警告报复，一边表示愿重启外交谈判，试图提高美以动武的代价。选举结束后，美以是否重启军事行动成为焦点。 两周前“精准喊顶”的德银：科技股距离“长期趋势底部”还要“跌5%” 。德银两周前下调美股科技及大盘成长股评级后，科技股相对标普500其余成分股跑输12个百分点。如今该行指出，调整可能仍未结束。机构仓位快速降温，300亿美元抄底资金开始出现流出迹象。接下来，财报表现、资金流向及外部风险，将决定调整能否止步于结构性轮动。 高盛警告：美联储12月加不加息，市场可能都没准备好 。高盛仍将12月加息视为基准情景，但市场对加息的定价约为90%，重新计入完整25个基点的难度正在上升。与此同时，2027年AI资本开支预计达1.6万亿美元，债务融资需求与能源通胀风险仍未消退，AI相关信用利差也已扩大至年内最宽水平，美债收益率后续走向仍面临多空力量的反复拉扯。 AI交易何时止跌？市场盯着Meta“天量发债”背后的“囚徒困境” 。巴克莱认为，AI巨头争相提前融资形成“囚徒困境”，集体发债将推高融资成本，限制信用利差收窄。随着低评级债券风险上升、AI发行人信用分化加剧，融资供给能否被市场消化，将成为判断AI交易能否企稳的关键。 野村：AI军备竞赛有75%的概率继续，2027年存储芯片短缺已基本锁定 。野村认为，AI军备竞赛陷入难以退出的困局，科技巨头即使自由现金流承压，仍可能继续加码投资。报告预计，竞赛延续的概率约为75%，2027年存储器供应量和价格已通过长期协议基本锁定。融资市场关闭是打破竞赛的主要风险，电力短缺则可能推迟芯片部署，但未必改变长期需求。 SemiAnalysis创始人深度解析：AI投资还能撑多久？英伟达护城河还能守住吗？内存荒何时结束？ Dylan Patel指出，AI基建扩张面临融资成本和芯片供应瓶颈，相关限制可能延续至2028年。英伟达的性能优势仍在，但自研芯片竞争可能逐步影响其市场份额和定价能力；内存行业的高利润能否维持，则取决于2028年后新增产能投放及供需变化。 行业 /概念 1、 教育 | 据上证报报道，国务院办公厅日前印发《关于适应人工智能技术发展助力构建就业友好型发展方式的意见》。意见要求，积极增强人工智能创造就业机会、赋能传统岗位、提升就业质量、激发创业活力的正面效应，有效减缓人工智能应用就业替代影响。意见提出，鼓励普通高校、职业学校(含技工院校)加快动态优化学科专业设置，超常规布局人工智能领域急需学科专业。实施人工智能专项培训计划。深入实施“技能照亮前程”培训行动。 2、 快递物流 | 据上证报报道，10月22日至23日，国家邮政局在河南洛阳召开邮政快递业安全治理规范化座谈会。会议强调，持续深入推进“反内卷”工作。要确保末端派费稳定，深化成本核算指导，严肃整治跨区揽件行为，企业总部要优化对所属服务网络的考核管理规则，不得层层加码、转嫁经营成本。 3、 词元概念/Token | 据上证报报道，上证资讯10月23日从北京市经济和信息化局获悉，截至目前，北京人工智能核心产业规模超过4500亿元，核心企业数量超过2500家，独角兽企业数量占全国半数以上，豆包、GLM、Kimi等基座模型能力全球领先。北京市将提升词元供给能力，制定北京市词元工厂分级评价标准，建设世界级词元工厂集群，提升高质量词元供给能力；还将出台词元分发平台评估标准，打造国际一流的词元分发交易平台。 4、 氦气 | 据中证报报道，当地时间10月23日，美国能源部宣布，已根据《2020年能源法》将氦气认定为关键材料，以加强美国制造业和供应链安全。美国能源部作出的这一决定，使氦气成为了该机构指定的第20种关键材料，并将这种工业气体纳入《2020年能源法》的关键材料框架，包括接受更严格的政府监管。 5、 云计算数据中心 | 据中证报报道，亚马逊首席执行官安迪·贾西（Andy Jassy）周五表示，受人工智能（AI）基础设施需求不断增长的影响，亚马逊网络服务（AWS）的云计算容量在2027年底前已基本售罄，且大量订单已排至2028年。贾西表示，亚马逊AWS正在努力快速扩展基础设施，以满足人工智能实验室和企业源源不断的需求。 6、 工业互联网 | 据中证报报道，CEIC2026消费电子创新大会22日至24日在深圳举行。其间，工业互联网操作系统产业联盟在2026消费电子创新大会·具身智能产业论坛上成立。业内人士表示，具身智能落地工厂，需要打通设计域-制造域、管理域-控制域两条业务链路，实现人、机、料、工艺、环境全要素集成。工业互联网操作系统需要满足跨域跨平台设计、任务可信运行、模型迁移一致性、多硬件设备适配四大核心需求。 7、 网络安全 | 据证券时报报道，前不久，全球网络安全界经历了最暗黑的48小时，大量AI智能体入侵美国银行，PHP漏洞导致大量国家政府网站关闭；10月23日，OpenAI和Anthropic，竟在同一天主动自曝：他们的前沿AI模型，在内部测试中双双“越狱”了。随着大模型与智能体等AI应用在政务、金融、工业、医疗及企业内部管理等场景加速落地，AI带来安全风险随之向业务核心环节渗透，也衍生出了提示词注入、模型投毒、多智能体协同欺骗等全新系统性风险。 8、 电力体制改革 | 据证券时报报道，全球最大“电力超市”正式开业，标志全国统一电力市场体系建设取得重大突破。统一电力市场建成后，跨区域电力交易规模有望持续扩容，现货交易、辅助服务交易常态化推进，对电力调度、交易仿真、计量采集、负荷管理等软硬件配套需求持续释放。 今日关注 中国 第二十届中央委员会第五次全体会议召开。 上交所与中证指数修订后的上证系列指数正式实施。 articles.title: 价格打折，哪些股票超跌了？
articles.summary: 双十一，股市也开启了“打折促销”。近期市场快速调整，创业板指从4372点回落到2700点以下，科创综指来到1300附近。不少前期热门股票大幅回撤，以历史高点为参照，中际旭创、新易盛、东山精密等热门股价格已跌至约四折。 尽管10月23日市场明显反弹，但科技成长板块此前的调整幅度已经不小，也引发了市场对科技股是否会重演周期股大幅波动的担忧。 股票毕竟不是普通商品，价格打折不等于估值便宜。 从交易层面看，下跌太快，股价反而可能出现反弹。但这类交易性反弹，并不是我们要讨论的“超跌”。 我们所说“超跌”是基于完整盈利周期基础上的估值便宜。 投资者在这个价格上购买股票，可能会输掉一些时间，但不会丧失本金。 为此，我们拿出光伏，锂电的龙头，跟光通信龙头进行比较。光伏和锂电都有完整的周期可以参考。 通过选取隆基绿能、宁德时代和中际旭创作为典型案例，比较不同景气阶段下的盈利和估值变化，观察经历大幅调整后，当前股价是否已经出现估值超跌。 看PE、PB的历史分位，不能判断估值 股价大幅调整后，市场通常把PE、PB放到历史的维度里去比较 ：当前低于历史多少分位，就说股票有多便宜。 例如，仅看原始PE的分布，宁德时代截至今年9月30日，15.85倍的pe低于此前五年20个季度的全部观测值；中际旭创当前32倍估值处于历史40%分位水平。单看历史估值，宁德时代似乎已经比较便宜，中际旭创也不算贵。 但问题是，这一估值背后所对应的盈利并不相同。 对于景气波动较大的公司，历史估值分位未必能反映真实的估值水平。仅是用历史分位，很难判断在周期中，是否真的“超跌”。 行业景气高低点，企业盈利水平差异明显 周期股在景气高点和低谷的盈利差异往往很大。即期估值容易受到利润波动的影响。 把三家公司利润放在一起来进行对比，通过年末EPS和ROE的观察，对周期差异就有更直观的感觉。 隆基2022年末ROE还有23.8%，2026年二季度却降至-15.5%，EPS也转为负数；中际旭创2021年末ROE只有7.6%，2026年二季度已超过51%，EPS从约1元增至13.4元；宁德时代的EPS则从2021年末约4.3元增加到2026年二季度约17.1元。 景气高点，利润增长会压低PE；景气低谷，利润收缩甚至亏损，又会使PE大幅抬升或失去参考意义。这就是单看即期PE容易踩的“坑”。 因此，仅凭PE、PB的历史分位，难以准确判断股价是否超跌。 我们尝试以历史稳态ROE为基准，还原企业在正常盈利水平下的估值，进一步观察当前股价是否具备安全边际。 估值是否合理，需要考虑完整的景气周期 经历大幅调整后， 优质公司的股价是否已经跌至具有吸引力的位置，需要从完整的行业景气周期出发，以正常盈利水平为参照。 我们采用历史ROE中位数作为稳态盈利水平，据此测算修正后的EPS和PE，观察企业在正常盈利能力下的历史估值区间，进而判断当前股价是否具备估值安全边际。 三家公司，三个答案 我们以三家公司各自的盈利周期起始日为起点，选取此后26个季度的ROE（TTM）中位数作为稳态盈利参考，并据此修正历史EPS和PE。 这样剔除不同景气阶段盈利波动对PE的影响，在相对统一的盈利水平下，观察市场过去给予企业的估值是否合理。 隆基绿能：便宜的前提，是先把利润赚回来 隆基的历史样本为2016Q1—2022Q2。26个季度的ROE中位数为19.53%，对应的标准化PE中位数为26.43倍。 问题是，隆基目前仍在亏损，负PE已经没法正常比较。按2026Q3的11.21元股价倒推：如果未来ROE恢复到约7.22%，对应PE为26.43倍；如果恢复到历史中位数19.53%，对应PE约9.76倍。 对隆基来说，能不能恢复盈利、能恢复到什么水平，比股价跌了多少更重要。 宁德时代：把盈利调回常态后，估值仍偏低 宁德的历史样本为2018Q2—2024Q3。ROE中位数为13.48%，标准化PE中位数为49.12倍，历史25%—75%区间为36.79—81.43倍。 2026Q3，宁德时代PE为15.85倍。把当期ROE折回13.48%后，修正PE约26.64倍，仍低于历史区间下沿，处在历史约3.8%分位。 换句话说，宁德的低PE并不只是当下盈利较高造成的。即使用历史中位数ROE来算，估值相对过去仍然偏低，具备一定的历史估值吸引力。 中际旭创：PE不高，不代表安全垫已经很厚 中际的历史样本为2020Q1—2026Q2。ROE中位数为10.73%，标准化PE中位数为61.95倍。 只看当前32倍PE，它处在原始PE历史约34.6%分位，处于较低分位水平。但如果用历史ROE中位数来折算，当前示意标准化PE约153倍，处于历史约84.6%分位，超过历史中间50%区间。 两种口径之所以差这么多，关键在于对高ROE能持续多久的判断。 如果未来ROE逐渐回到历史水平，当前价格在这套模型下没有明显的绝对吸引力；但如果AI光模块需求带来的高盈利能维持较长时间，用10.73%的历史ROE做假设又可能过于保守。 跌下来以后，究竟怎样才算便宜？ 三家公司给出了不同的答案：宁德时代在盈利还原至历史中枢后，估值仍处于历史较低分位；隆基绿能的估值吸引力取决于盈利修复；中际旭创则需要关注当前高ROE的持续性。 从跨周期估值角度看，判断股价是否超跌，不能仅依据股价回撤幅度或短期交易性反弹，更需要考察企业在稳态盈利水平下的估值位置。 若盈利回归常态后，估值仍明显偏高，说明当前价格对盈利回落的风险反映可能不足；若在相对保守的盈利假设下，估值仍处于历史低位，则可能具备一定的安全边际，但仍需结合基本面判断折价是否合理。 不过需要注意的是，历史中位数不能代替未来盈利预测，行业景气和公司竞争力也可能发生变化。但把价格与可持续的赚钱能力放在一起看，至少能避免把“跌得多”直接当成“够便宜”。 股价打了几折不重要。重要的是，利润回到正常水平以后，价格是否依然合理。 本文来源： 东吴证券陈李、葛晓媛 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: AI势头回落并非牛熊分界
articles.summary: AI趋势回落并非熊市开端，非AI可能反而会面临更为有利的环境 1）产业趋势回落≠牛转熊。A股在过往存在比较广泛的“产业趋势回落=牛转熊”的思维，核心是过往的产业趋势（2006~2007年的工业与金融、2009年的地产与基建、2013~2015年的移动互联、2019~2021年的能源转型等）对其他经济部门带来广泛的拉动作用。而本轮AI产业的进展，至少在短期内对其他经济部门产生了不少挤出效应，包括导致了物料和资源价格暴涨、推动了债券市场供需紧张和长债利率大幅飙升、一定程度上挤出就业，财富效应的增长极为失衡，市场分化的程度历史罕见，甚至出现了所谓“硅基世界”和“碳基世界”的对立。这也意味着，过往“产业趋势行情结束=牛转熊”的经验可能并不适用于这轮AI硬件主导的行情，非AI的不少板块早已步入下行趋势，而AI只不过最后“补跌”。 2）AI短期内对其他部门产生了负外部性，若AI势头回落，一些非AI板块反而可能有转机。目前已经显性化的负外部性至少包含三类：第一，电子元器件、电力等基础生活物资的大幅涨价，抬高生产和生活成本，压抑其他领域需求，典型的如消费电子；第二，算力基础设施投建推动私人部门巨额债务融资，推升全球无风险利率，对所有高利率敏感性的需求产生冲击；第三，挤出就业，尤其是对于年轻人就业的影响，比如根据斯坦福与ADP就业数据库今年9月最新数据，自动化型AI使用占比最高职业组的22~25岁就业较2022年11月下降10.9%，最低组同期上升7.8%。这些因素引发了实体经济和市场的剧烈分化，但反过来看，如果AI投资的速度在未来有所放缓，非AI板块可能也不会面临如此负面的宏观环境，比如无风险利率出现大幅回落。事实上，从当前的美债定价来看，10年期美债利率的走向与北美AI硬件股的股价走势高度相关，如果未来出现持续性的回落，至少对海外的非AI部门需求可能产生促进。 估值收缩的进程今年已基本完成，行情宽度有望逐步拓展 1）AI的二阶导修正、非AI的估值收缩，都有望在今年基本完成。AI完成了第一波“二阶导”修正。与2021年底至2022年4月底的新能源行情调整类似，本轮AI同样是在产业景气仍在、增速预期转弱时提前下修估值。从估值收缩的视角出发，本轮AI硬件的估值压缩幅度已与2022年新能源第一轮调整相当。根据Wind数据，7月1日以来，电子与通信板块整体法PE（TTM）从74.0倍压缩至42.4倍，降幅42.8%；2022年新能源第一轮调整（2021年12月17日-2022年4月26日），电力设备及新能源板块市值下PE从51.2倍压缩至27.8倍，降幅45.7%。站在全球对比的视角下，A股非AI板块处于全球估值洼地。我们用中、美、日、韩四个市场的AI与非AI龙头篮子，以整体法测算PE（TTM）并进行跨市场对比。截至10月22日，A股是唯一一个AI相对非AI估值溢价仍高于历史中枢的市场：AI/非AI的PE倍数为4.4倍，处于2016年以来82%的分位，美、日、韩的这一倍数则分别回落至1%、17%、24%的分位。美、日非AI非金融龙头的PE分别为33.5倍和23.0倍，处于98%和95%的分位；A股非AI非金融龙头只有15.6倍，处于历史21%分位，消费、制造、医药龙头分别只处于12%、1%、3%的分位。当然，低估值源于疲弱的内需以及市场对非AI领域外需的潜在担忧（贸易摩擦、海外高利率、高油价等），有其合理性。但换个角度看，这种导致低估值的悲观，很大程度上源于今年的现实与年初市场期待的巨大割裂，投资者难以预料在“十五五”的第一年广义财政赤字会意外转为大幅负增长、市场从美联储降息预期转为加息预期、10年期美债利率创了2007年以来新高、中欧贸易摩擦突然升温、美伊战争爆发且持续快一年。这种落差，是导致不少非AI板块在今年业绩增长亮眼的情况下估值发生剧烈收缩的原因。当下，至少市场已经充分认知到了这些宏观负面因素，无论是海外利率还是国内政策，任何边际上超预期的变化可能都有助于改变当下A股相对于全球市场更为悲观的估值体系。 2）K型分化逐步收敛，行情宽度有望逐步拓展。对于AI侧，商业化空间增长焦虑还将继续约束AI投资单年度的绝对规模体量，同时加深市场对于未来“一阶导”拐点的警惕，AI对于非AI板块的虹吸很难再出现，同时考虑到主流机构资金仍然超配TMT板块，市场反弹过程中的持仓均衡化过程也将制约AI板块的弹性。我们看到，在本周市场止跌企稳的过程中，率先反弹的AI新技术是筹码出清相当彻底且机构持仓比例低的机器人板块，而非算力基建相关的板块。对非AI板块，当下几乎所有的负面因素都已经被市场所认知（即便可能并未完全定价），在经历一轮系统性调整后，低预期本身就是有利的条件。以出海板块为例，中欧贸易摩擦已经摆在台面上，未来每年的规则修订谈判和博弈可能是常态化的，企业最终还是会凭借强大的竞争优势适应；人民币在明年只要升值速度有所放缓，汇兑损失就会同比减少，就会带来净利润率的回升；美国中期选举后民主党如果控制国会，中东战争格局可能会有积极变化，所带来的油价影响可能边际上转弱；AI投资增速放缓，带来海外长端无风险利率回落，对非AI行业的需求抑制作用减弱。由于这些负面因素在今年已经被投资者系统性认知，只要后续有边际上的好转，对非AI板块本身也产生促进。 资金面的出清需要时间，PB-ROE 代表的稳健回报型策略可能更加占优 资金面快速恶化的过程大概率已接近尾声，在本周ETF明显放量的信号下，主动买盘开始谨慎流入市场，融资盘去杠杆的负向循环被阻断。截至10月21日，两市融资余额已回落至2.45万亿元，相对年内高点累计减少5600亿元，降幅18.6%，已回到去年11月下旬的水平，交易层面的降温更为明显，融资买入额占两市成交额的比例（MA5，下同）6月平均为9.86%，7月降至8.99%，9月为8.66%，10月以来进一步降至8.01%，10月16日读数7.84%，为2024年9月以来的最低值，低于“9.24”行情前约9%的水平。活跃私募的仓位同样回到低位，对中信证券渠道调研显示，样本活跃私募仓位8月7日当周以来持续回落，10月16日已降至67.5%，为2024年3月以来最低，较76.3%的历史中位数低8.8个百分点。虽然资金面指标已经回落到较低的位置，但彻底出清并开始持续改善仍然需要时间，这个阶段动量和景气策略会持续弱势，市场轮动速度加快，而以PB-ROE外代表的低估值质量型策略会更占优。目前有两类行业在明年满足这样的框架，一类是具备高股息率和稳健盈利增速的品种，如白电、纺织服装、食品调味、火电等，另一类是带有供给出清潜力逻辑的品种，如油运、快递物流、头部地产开发商、部分锂电材料、石化偏中游的环节等。 articles.title: SemiAnalysis创始人深度解析：AI投资还能撑多久？英伟达护城河还能守住吗？内存荒何时结束？
articles.summary: AI基础设施投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本上升、半导体供应链受限与自研芯片竞争加剧，正在共同考验这轮AI热潮的持续性。 在10月23日于美国举行的CASPA第35届年度大会上，SemiAnalysis创始人兼CEO Dylan Patel、Bernstein董事总经理兼高级分析师 Stacy Rasgon，以及Austin Lyons围绕半导体行业前景展开讨论，重点涉及AI基础设施投资、供应链瓶颈与芯片竞争格局。 Patel指出， 当前AI算力需求依然旺盛，但基板、内存等关键环节的产能约束，正在限制基础设施扩张。 与此同时，融资成本大幅攀升，缺乏长期客户订单的新兴云服务商越来越难以获得资金，AI投资能否持续推进，不仅取决于需求，也取决于项目的融资能力与回报。 对于英伟达，Rasgon认为，其产品性能提升仍能支撑较高售价，但云厂商自研芯片正在改变竞争格局。 随着Google TPU、亚马逊Trainium以及OpenAI等企业的自研芯片计划推进，英伟达即使继续增长，也可能面临市场份额和定价能力的双重压力。 内存市场则面临另一重考验：HBM需求旺盛、行业利润率处于高位，但厂商扩产可能在2028年后逐步改变供需关系。未来两年，融资能力、关键零部件供给与自研芯片的竞争，将成为影响AI基础设施扩张速度和产业链利润分配的关键变量。 华尔街见闻总结要点如下： AI投资仍有增长空间，但融资成本正成为重要约束。 美国10年期国债收益率突破5%，部分新兴云服务商无担保债券收益率接近15%。缺乏长期客户订单的企业融资难度更大，项目建设节奏将越来越取决于融资能力与投资回报。 半导体供应链瓶颈短期难解，基板与内存是关键制约。 基板、HBM、光学互联组件及洁净室产能均面临供应限制。相比之下，电力短缺可通过现场发电等方式部分缓解，半导体供应链扩产则需要更长时间。 内存短缺可能延续至新增产能释放，2028年后供需格局面临转折。 HBM需求旺盛，内存行业毛利率据称已达88%—90%；但如果新增产能在2028年后集中投产，而需求增速放缓，内存价格与利润率可能承压。 英伟达仍有性能优势，但自研芯片正在挑战其定价权。 英伟达持续通过性能提升支撑高售价，但Google
